L43: * * *
L44: ### Historical Note
L45: 
L46: The School of Mathematics was the first School established by the Institute. It has also become the largest. Founding Institute Director Abraham Flexner explained the decision to establish this School first, because mathematics "(1) was fundamental...(2) required the least investment in plant or books... (3) [and there was] greater agreement upon personnel in the field of mathematics than in any other subject.". ^{1}
L47: Mathematician Oswald Veblen, among the close advisers to Flexner, was the first Faculty appointment to the School of Mathematics, effective October 1, 1932. In the fall term of 1933, the School officially began its work in loaned space on the Princeton University campus in Fine Hall, now Jones Hall, with roughly thirty participants, including Faculty and visiting scholars.
L48: The promise of establishing a close relationship in both the short- and long-term between mathematicians at the Institute and Princeton University had been a determining factor in locating the Institute in Princeton, New Jersey.
L49: By the beginning of 1935, Veblen had been joined on the School's Faculty by James Alexander, Albert Einstein, Marston Morse, John von Neumann, and Hermann Weyl. Each represented intellectual excellence and diversity in the field of mathematics—though being rooted in the same overall discipline also resulted in essential interconnections and overlap. Some of the early Faculty, von Neumann and Weyl in particular, represented uniquely eclectic approaches.
L50: The Faculty was also chosen for their ability to be magnets for other scholars. This would be essential to support the central purpose of the Institute as a haven for short-term independent study. The intellectual climate of the School also fostered more structured opportunities for learning, including seminars and courses. In addition, there were scheduled times for presentations and discussion afforded by the Mathematics Club.
L51: In 1939, the Institute's own campus was established, so that the School was able to move to the new Fuld Hall, retaining only a minor presence in Fine Hall for several more years. Despite the move, as had been hoped, intellectual exchange and collaboration between mathematicians at the Institute and Princeton University remained vital. For roughly the School's first decade, the composition of the Faculty was stable even as a steady stream of scholars came and went.
L52: In the late 1940s and 1950s, as the original Faculty members retired or died, new appointments were made -- such as Atle Selberg (1951), Deane Montgomery (1951), Armand Borel (1957), and André Weil (1958) -- that would carry the School through the next several decades.
L53: In the late 1970s, the School looked back over its history and described its work until then as follows: "Reflecting the interests of the permanent Faculty over time, the School has been primarily concerned with five areas broadly understood: topology; analysis and global analysis; Lie groups, algebraic groups, automorphic functions and number theory; algebraic geometry; and logic".
L54: ^{2} In addition to these core areas of study, until the creation of the School of Natural Sciences in 1965, the School of Mathematics did in fact pursue the study of mathematics using an especially wide scope, so that the natural sciences, especially mathematical physics, has been a fundamental part of the intellectual development of the Institute.
L55: The two Schools have found it mutually beneficial to continue working cooperatively in the field of mathematical physics—to mention just one area of such collaboration.
L56: While the number of active Faculty in the School of Mathematics has grown only modestly over the years to a total of eight in 2017, appointments have provided occasions to stretch the intellectual scope of the School into fields traditionally less represented by the Faculty. One example was the 1986 appointment of Thomas Spencer, whose work incorporates applied mathematics, whereas the intellectual mainstay of the School has been chiefly in pure mathematics.
L57: In contrast to the number of Faculty, the number of visiting scholars has seen more significant growth over the years. By the 2010s, it was common for the School to invite fifty to sixty scholars per academic year with that number increasing to nearly one-hundred when categories such as short-term visitor and long-term appointments factor in. The School of Mathematics is one of only eight Mathematical Sciences Institutes supported nationwide by the National Science Foundation.
L58: In addition to hosting visiting scholars, the School has historically found other means by which to encourage scholarship in the field of mathematics. Beginning in 1933, , the leading mathematical journal in the United States, began joint publication by the Institute and Princeton University. This collaboration continues through today.
L59: In the 1960s, the School established "Special Years," as they are now often called, based upon a "promising" ^{3} topic intended to attract a nexus of scholars within the School, while continuing to place major emphasis on support of mathematicians studying across the spectrum of the field. The initiative lapsed for a time due to lack of financial resources, but was revived in the 1980s.
L60: Examples of Special Years include: Statistical Mechanics and Stochastic Geometry (1997-1998) and Galois Representations and Automorphic Forms (2010-2011). In the early 1980s, the School initiated the Hermann Weyl Lectures, which are presented on an irregular basis. Past presenters of these Lectures, which are published in the , include Clifford Henry Taubes (2002) and János Kollár (2007).
L61: The seminars, courses, and other structured learning opportunities established from the earliest days of the School have been continued. An example of seminars are those in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics. The School's presence in fields related to these disciplines had lapsed since the days of Faculty members Kurt Gödel and John von Neumann.
L62: The seminars began on an exploratory basis in the early 1990's, and took firm hold with their success and the appointment to the Faculty of Avi Wigderson in 1999.
L63: The field of mathematics faces systemic challenges in regard to inclusivity. The School has invited women from the beginning, but a program administered by the School directly addresses the hurdles faced by women mathematicians.
L64: Established in 1994, the Mentoring Program for Women in Mathematics (renamed, in 2006, the Program for Women and Mathematics) annually hosts women mathematicians, including those at the undergraduate level, for an "intensive 11-day mentoring program." ^{5} Another program administered by the Institute provides an outlet for those with limited access to the academy.
L65: The IAS/Park City Mathematics Program (PCMI), affiliated with the IAS since 1993, has various components that provide opportunities for independent and collective study and includes a three-week residential summer session. A key component of PCMI is the opportunity to build relationships between mathematicians at various stages of their career.
L66: In 1993, there were two new buildings completed on the Institute campus (the first significant construction since 1969). One was the new home of the School of Mathematics. It features seminar rooms and a common room in addition to enough office space to bring most of the School's visiting scholars, Faculty, and staff under one roof. The School has also retained a presence in Fuld Hall, including the Mathematics-Natural Sciences Library.
L67: In 1999, the so-called Math Building was rededicated as Simonyi Hall in honor of generous contributions by IAS Trustee Dr. Charles Simonyi to the School of Mathematics.

L97: ### Related Materials
L98: #### Related Materials
L99: Further information relating to those represented in the Members, Visitors, Assistants series can be found in various locations. For short-term visitors, especially those without files, minimal information can sometimes be found in the School's Faculty Meeting Minutes in the School of Mathematics records. For scholars in the natural sciences before 1965, also see the School of Natural Sciences's People series. For all visiting scholars, files have also been created and maintained by the Director's Office.
L100: Within the record group for that office, please see the following series, as appropriate: Members files, Visitors files, and Assistants files. In the rare case that a scholar also served on the Institute's Board of Trustees, the record group for that body may provide additional materials.
L101: For the School in general, the Records of the Office of the Director-Director's Office School Files series will contain some materials both duplicating the School's own records and unique to the collection. The set of Faculty Meeting Minutes originating with the Director's Office is less comprehensive than the set from the School itself, but the folders that include meeting Agendas dating from 1953-1987 are unique.

L36: ### Scope and Contents note
L37: 
L38: Files of IAS members are periodically added to this series. All current and past Schools of the Institute are represented by the scholars in the series. Contents of these files may include applications, letters of reference, invitation letters, and correspondence related to administrative matters such as travel and housing. In some cases there is correspondence related to a Member's activities after leaving the Institute.
L39: The vast majority of the series concerns those who accepted the Institute invitations, but there are some declinations and, in a few cases, people who died before arriving at the Institute. Files may not reflect all visits by a person to the Institute, especially for those with additional visits that took place after 1989.
L40: Some files or portions of files pertain to visits to the Institute that were not Memberships, including for people who served as assistants to various Institute Faculty members and were offered academic term and summer visitorships.

L68: ### Related Materials
L69: #### Related Archival Materials note
L70: While this series contains files for thousands of people who visited the Institute, it does not include files for everyone who came to the Institute as a Member. For the most part, the files of those who came to the Institute as Members originally and were later appointed to the Faculty were moved to the Records of the Office of the Director: Faculty files series, though there are some exceptions.
L71: Files for those who came to the Institute primarily as Visitors or Assistants are in the Records of the Office of the Director: Visitor and Assistant files series.
L72: The files in this series were maintained by the Director's Office. The Institute's Schools also often kept separate files on their Members. These files are found in the record groups corresponding to an individual Member's School of affiliation.
